title: What does "good" mean? Performance functions

slides.title: What does "good" mean? Performance functions
slides.notes: The network minimises exactly what we tell it to. Today: choosing what to tell it, and how to check the result.

runs.text: Choice of performance function · Post-training analysis
Artificial Neural Networks (SETE08) · Unit 5: Applications and Case Studies

slides.title: The network minimises what you ask it to
slides.notes: Everyday parallel: if a delivery rider is paid only per delivery, speed wins over care. People and networks both optimise what is measured.

runs.text: The network minimises what you ask it to
It is the definition of success
Training changes the weights to make one number as small as possible. That number is the performance function.
A wrong measure, a wrong model
Ask for "fewest wrong answers" on payments where 1 in 100 is fraud, and the best answer is to call nothing fraud.
Fitting, classification and noisy data each need a different function. The output layer must match it too.
Choosing the performance function is choosing what the network will care about.

slides.title: Mean square error: the default for fitting
slides.notes: Hagan presents the Minkowski error with exponent K: K = 2 gives MSE, K = 1 gives mean absolute error, which is more robust to outliers.

runs.text: Mean square error: the default for fitting
Q examples. t: target. a: network output. Averaged over all examples and all outputs.
Why it is the usual choice for numbers
Smooth and easy to differentiate, which backpropagation needs.
Squaring punishes large misses far more than small ones: a 10-minute error costs 100, a 2-minute error costs 4.
Pairs with a linear output neuron.
Weakness: a few wild records dominate. For data with outliers use the mean absolute error instead.

slides.title: Cross-entropy: the choice for classification
slides.notes: With MSE and a saturated sigmoid the gradient is nearly zero exactly when the network is confidently wrong, so it learns slowly from its worst mistakes.

runs.text: Targets t are 0 or 1 (one-of-N). Outputs a are softmax probabilities. Only the true class contributes.
It scores the probability given to the right class
Output 0.9 for the true class costs 0.11. Output 0.1 costs 2.3. Output 0.01 costs 4.6.
Being confidently wrong is punished without limit.
With a softmax output the gradient is simply a − t: it does not vanish when the network is badly wrong.
The trained outputs can be read as probabilities.

slides.title: The cost of being confidently wrong
slides.notes: Ask: a fraud model says 2% for a payment that is fraud. Which cost function will make it fix that fastest?

runs.text: The cost of being confidently wrong

ops.xTitle: Output a given to the true class (target = 1)

runs.text: The true class is 1. What does each function charge?
Squared error never charges more than 1, however wrong the output.
Cross-entropy climbs steeply as the output approaches 0.
So cross-entropy pushes hardest on the examples the network gets most wrong.
Near a = 1 both are small: they agree when the network is right.

slides.title: Regularisation: penalise large weights
slides.notes: In deep learning this is called weight decay or L2 regularisation. Hagan Chapter 13 derives the Bayesian version; here we only need the idea.

runs.text: First term: the usual sum of squared errors on the data. Second term: the sum of all squared weights.
Small weights give a smooth function
A network needs large weights to make sharp bends between data points.
Penalising weight size keeps the response smooth, so it follows the pattern, not the noise.
The ratio α / β sets the strength: too large and the network underfits.
Bayesian regularisation sets α and β automatically during training.
It is an alternative to early stopping, and needs no validation set.

slides.title: What the penalty does to the fit
slides.notes: Students can reproduce this in the Battery Oracle station by adding neurons and then switching regularisation on.

runs.text: What the penalty does to the fit
Same network and data, with and without the penalty
Without the penalty a large network threads through every noisy point.
With it the curve stays close to the true pattern.
The training error is slightly higher with the penalty. The test error is much lower.
Too much penalty flattens the curve: check both errors.

slides.title: Committees of networks
slides.notes: Disagreement among the members is also useful: where they disagree strongly, the input is probably unlike the training data.

runs.text: Train 5 to 10 networks from different random starts, or on different divisions of the data. You were going to restart anyway.
For fitting, average the outputs. For classification, average the probabilities or take a vote.
Each network makes different mistakes. Averaging cancels part of them, so the committee usually beats its best member.
Like taking a second and third medical opinion. The cost is several times the computing at run time.

slides.title: The fraud detector that was 99% accurate
slides.notes: Let the class work out the arithmetic before showing the next slide. This is a composite teaching story, not one named company.

runs.text: The fraud detector that was 99% accurate
A payments team trains a network on 10,000 transactions. It reports 99% accuracy. Everyone is pleased.
A month after launch, fraud losses have not fallen at all.
Someone finally counts: of 100 frauds in the test data, the model caught none. It had learnt to say "genuine" every time.
How can a model be 99% accurate and useless? What should the team have measured?
UPI Fraud Alarm: press Break to see the 99% model, then open the confusion matrix.

slides.title: Counting what "99% accurate" hides
slides.notes: This 2 by 2 table is the confusion matrix. L39 builds sensitivity, specificity and the ROC curve from it.

runs.text: Fraud caught: 0 of 100. The one number that mattered is zero.
Accuracy rewards the common class. With rare events it says almost nothing.
Measure what the business cares about: frauds caught, and false alarms raised.
Then train so that the rare class counts: balance the data or weight its errors.

slides.title: Reading the three errors
slides.notes: This table reappears in L40 for overfitting and extrapolation. It is a frequent exam question.

rows.text: Training, validation and test errors all high
Add neurons; restart from new weights
Training low; validation and test much higher
Early stopping, regularise, fewer neurons, more data
Training and validation low; test much higher
Test data lies outside the training range
Collect data that covers those cases
All three low and close together
Use it, within the range of the data

runs.text: All three low still says nothing about situations that none of the three sets contain.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.notes: Marks are usually split between the formulas and the reasoning for when to use each.

runs.text: Discuss the choice of performance function for neural network training. How does regularisation improve generalisation?
Mean square error: formula, use in fitting, sensitivity to outliers.
Cross-entropy: formula, softmax output, why it suits classification.
Regularisation: add the sum of squared weights to the error; small weights give smooth functions.
Committees of networks: averaging several trained networks.
Why the measure must match the problem: the 99% accuracy example.

slides.notes: Bridge: we have one tool so far, the three errors. Next hour adds a specific tool for each task type.

runs.text: With a linear output. Mean absolute error when outliers are present.
With softmax or sigmoid outputs that read as probabilities.
Regularisation and committees both improve generalisation.
Their pattern tells you which design step to revisit.
